changes.from: Trauma activates the cerebellum and brain stem, the "lizard brain", and sets off a survival alarm even when no physical threat is present. Because the prefrontal cortex, the logic center, is not yet fully developed, children express this inner alarm through outward behavior.
changes.to: Ongoing stress keeps the body's stress response system (the HPA axis) switched on. Over time it can set off at lower thresholds, and the brain areas for fear and quick reactions build more connections than the areas for reasoning, planning and self-control (National Scientific Council on the Developing Child, Working Paper 3).

changes.from: A review of studies on outdoor play found that children who had more chances for risky play were more physically active, and that it supported their social skills, creativity and resilience. Most injuries were minor (Brussoni and colleagues, 2015).
changes.to: A review of 18 studies found that risky outdoor play went with more physical activity and better social skills, and that rough and tumble play did not make children more aggressive (Brussoni and colleagues, 2015).

changes.from: Their review of 21 studies found that risky outdoor play goes with more physical activity and better social health, that climbing at height did not raise the rate or severity of injuries in the studies reviewed, and that rough and tumble play did not make children more aggressive.
changes.to: Their review of 21 articles reporting 18 studies found that risky outdoor play goes with more physical activity and better social health, and that rough and tumble play did not make children more aggressive. One study found no link between the height of play equipment and injuries.
